subject: SSO — three enterprise asks queued, time to commit to architecture
body:
Rohan, Yelena —

We now have three enterprise customers (Hooli, Umbrella, Globex) where SSO is on the renewal critical path. We can't keep deferring. Time to commit to an architecture.

Question for the design phase: SAML, OIDC, or both? CSM team is hearing more demand for SAML (older enterprise). Engineering instinct from past chats has been OIDC.

Diego

subject: Re: SSO — three enterprise asks queued, time to commit to architecture
body:
OIDC-first, SAML supported. Both ship.

Rationale:
- OIDC is the cleaner spec. Library quality is better. New customers will use OIDC by default.
- SAML is the table-stakes spec for older enterprise IT. Refusing it costs us deals.
- Cost of supporting both: real but not 2x. The session model is the same; the assertion-handling layer is what differs.

Yelena's the right primary owner. I'll review. Sasha co-signs the security model.

What I'd push back on: a phased 'OIDC now, SAML later' approach. Once we ship OIDC and call it 'SSO support,' the SAML work loses urgency and we end up explaining for two years why we don't have it. Better to ship both, tag SAML beta, and have an honest 'we GA when we're confident' story.

Proposing RFC by end of Feb, design review first week of March, ship by end of Q3.

—r

title: ADR-0023: SSO architecture is OIDC-first with SAML supported
author: Yelena Petrov
body:
## Status
Accepted — 2024-03-07 architecture review.

## Context
Three enterprise customers (Hooli, Umbrella, Globex) are blocking on SSO. We need a unified architecture that covers OIDC and SAML without doubling our maintenance footprint.

## Decision
1. Unified session model. Both OIDC and SAML produce a Northwind session token; downstream services don't know which protocol authenticated.
2. OIDC primary path. Built first, gets GA designation at ship.
3. SAML supported, beta at ship, GA after first 3 production customers.
4. JIT (just-in-time) provisioning for both. SCIM provisioning is a separate ADR (ADR-0029, follow-up).
5. Identity provider compatibility: Okta, Azure AD, Google Workspace, generic SAML 2.0 / OIDC compliant.

## Consequences
+ Closes the three known enterprise deals.
+ Foundation for future SCIM and audit-log work.
+ Single session model means downstream services don't fork.
- SAML beta period requires customer-managed risk acceptance for early adopters. Sasha to draft customer comms.
- Increases attack surface; security review is a hard gate.

## Rejected alternatives
- 'OIDC only, ship SAML never' — would lose Globex (they're SAML-only on Okta).
- 'OIDC now, SAML in a future quarter' — Rohan's pushback per email thread.
- 'Use a third-party SSO vendor (e.g. WorkOS)' — evaluated. Rejected because we want first-class control of the session model and audit logs for compliance customers.

subject: Proposal: GraphQL public gateway for partner integrations
body:
Rohan, Devika —

Proposal for a public GraphQL gateway. Three partner integrations (Wonka POS, BluePeak commerce, BuyNLarge channels) are asking for flexible queries. REST means writing 4-6 endpoints per integration, GraphQL would let them shape the response. Estimated saves us 2-3 weeks of integration work per partner.

Want to land an RFC for this. Who'd be best to lead?

Diego

subject: Re: Proposal: GraphQL public gateway for partner integrations
body:
Going to want to dig in before committing review cycles.

The headline pushback I have: GraphQL on the public surface adds (a) per-query auth/authz complexity, (b) N+1 risk on naive client queries, (c) a second query language for our team to support, (d) tooling cost for partners (most have decent REST clients, fewer have decent GraphQL clients). The savings you describe are real, but they're concentrated in the second integration of each pattern, not the first.

Let me see the RFC. If the answer to 'why not REST with a few collection endpoints + sparse fieldsets' is convincing, I'll change my mind. If not, I'll push to kill.

—r

title: GraphQL gateway RFC — review
discussion:
Diego presented. RFC scope: GraphQL endpoint at api.northwind-saas.com/graphql, schema generated from existing service models, persisted-query allowlist for partners.

Rohan walked through pushbacks:
1. Persisted-query allowlist effectively makes this REST-with-extra-steps. If we control the query set, we don't need GraphQL — we need a small set of well-designed REST endpoints + sparse fieldsets.
2. The auth model gets messier: GraphQL fine-grained authz requires field-level decisions which our current authz layer doesn't model. We'd need new infrastructure.
3. The 2-3 weeks saved per partner is real, but the steady-state cost of carrying GraphQL is at least one engineer's quarterly attention. We'd need 4-6 partners per year minimum to break even, and we have 3 lined up.
4. Performance: N+1 risk on un-allowlisted queries (which the proposal allows for a dev-mode). Fixable with DataLoader, but adds yet another layer.

Diego conceded points 2 and 3. Pushed back on 1: 'sparse fieldsets are a poor man's GraphQL.' Rohan: 'agreed, and that's exactly why I think we should ship the poor man's version first.'

Devika asked Maya for an opinion. Maya: 'I think Rohan's right that we don't have the partner volume yet. I'd revisit when we have 6+ partners.'

Decision: kill the GraphQL RFC. Diego to write a sparse-fieldset extension to existing REST endpoints, scoped at 1 sprint.
decisions: DO: sparse-fieldsets on existing REST endpoints (Diego to scope, 1-sprint)

title: Graveyard: GraphQL public gateway (killed 2024-02-19)
author: Rohan Iyer
body:
## What was proposed
GraphQL public gateway for partner integrations. RFC by Diego, Jan 2024.

## Why it was killed
Not enough partner volume to amortize the operational cost. The savings were real (2-3 weeks per partner integration) but the steady-state carrying cost (one engineer's quarterly attention, new authz infrastructure) wasn't justified at our current 3-partner pipeline.

## Conditions to revisit
- 6+ active partner integrations OR
- A specific partner with a query pattern we genuinely cannot serve via REST + sparse fieldsets

## What we did instead
Sparse-fieldset extensions on existing REST endpoints. 1-sprint scope. Same flexibility-of-response value for the use case Diego cared about, no new infrastructure.

## Lesson
Don't add a query language. Add the smallest extension to the existing query language that solves the problem. We learned this with Mongo migration too — adding stores is more expensive than it looks. Same lesson for adding query layers.
